title: Notes from Mayport
author: Lexi Zotomayor
excerpt: Driven by itchy feet and a curiosity about local ghost stories, a former Pacific journalist finds an unexpected echo of island history—and a welcome dose of pelican-watching—in the old fishing village of Mayport, Florida.
bodyText:
When I first arrived in the contiguous United States, I had a bad case of itchy feet. I had stepped away from the newsroom, though my laptop was rarely idle as I sent stories out into the world and hoped for the best. I was also trying to get a small business off the ground—a venture nipped in the bud for reasons best left unsaid.

Through that unsettled stretch, I always had Mayport.

My excuses for driving out there were plain enough: fresh seafood at Safe Harbor, a bench to watch pelicans act like pelicans, and a mild curiosity about a house everyone swore was haunted. Still, the fishing village at the edge of Jacksonville felt remarkably like home. Travel has a way of holding up a mirror, showing how our daily whims are often steered by old memories.

Looking into the lore behind that haunted house sent me down a much deeper rabbit hole of local history. Mayport, as it happens, has been keeping time for a very long while. Long before French Huguenots landed in 1562—only to be shooed away by the Spanish—the Timucuan people lived along these shores. Archaeologists have traced human life here across ten millennia and nine distinct eras.

The Timucua might have held their ground had they possessed immunity to the ship-borne diseases their visitors carried. Instead, invisible epidemics nearly wiped them out. Reading that, I thought immediately of the Pacific Islanders of Guam, the Marianas, and Kosrae, who suffered the exact same fate. Foreigners scarcely needed muskets or swords; their microscopic stowaways did the work for them, slipping ashore unseen to claim the vulnerable one by one.

Over dinner at Safe Harbor, however, my mind took a lighter turn. Picking through a plate of fried fish, I pictured defeated French sailors packing their gear for the trip back across the Atlantic while Spanish flags went up over the dunes.

Mayport does not brag with towering monuments, though it keeps a few relics from the late nineteenth century. There is the lighthouse, and there is the Presbyterian Church, standing on its corner since 1892. Local notes left by Helen Cooper Floyd tell us it was first christened the Addie Fatio Community Chapel, named for a local parishioner.

Then there is the William Joseph King House, good for a stray goosebump or two. Even Mr. King left behind accounts of uncanny run-ins with spirits who seemed in no hurry to vacate the premises.

When the ghost stories grow too thick, the pelicans offer an instant cure. They gather by the dozens near the Safe Harbor parking lot, where anyone with a camera can spend an easy afternoon watching them glide in for clumsy landings or preen unbothered a few feet away.

Mayport sits easily between what was and what is—a modest outpost on the water that welcomes the present without forgetting its past.
